name: Precinct Properties New Zealand
company_name: Precinct Properties New Zealand Limited & Precinct Properties Investments Limited (stapled)
overview: Precinct is New Zealand's largest owner, manager and developer of premium inner-city real estate, concentrated in Auckland and Wellington CBD office towers (PwC Tower, Commercial Bay, AON Centre, HSBC Tower, Bowen Campus, ANZ Centre-legacy assets) alongside a growing Precinct Flex co-working business, hotels, car parks and an expanding capital-partnering/funds-management platform. The entity trades as a stapled security combining Precinct Properties New Zealand Limited (property owner, 'PPNZ') and Precinct Properties Investments Limited (manager, 'PPIL'); fiscal year ends 30 June and results are reported in NZD.

business_model.summary: Core income is contracted rent from a premium, high-occupancy CBD office and retail portfolio (97% occupancy, 6.1yr WALT). Precinct is pivoting from a pure balance-sheet landlord to a capital-light 'own, develop, manage, partner' model: it recycles capital by selling down stabilised assets and part-interests in developments into partnerships with global institutional investors (GIC via Precinct Pacific Investment Limited Partnership/PPILP, and PAG on PwC Tower), retaining a minority stake plus asset/development/property management fees. This reduces balance-sheet capital intensity per dollar of assets under influence while preserving upside and control. Secondary streams are Precinct Flex (co-working/events, e.g. Pipiri Lane), hotel/hospitality income, and an emerging living-sector platform (build-to-rent, purpose-built student accommodation at 22 Stanley Street and 256 Queen Street). FFO is the key underlying earnings measure the company guides to and pays dividends against (target payout ratio ~90-92%).

revenue_streams.name: Investment property rental income (Auckland + Wellington office/retail)

business_model.customer_type: B2B — blue-chip corporate and government tenants (law firms, banks, professional services, NZ government agencies) plus institutional capital partners (GIC, PAG) and, in student accommodation, university/tertiary tenancy agreements
business_model.geographic_mix: Auckland CBD (majority, growing share via PwC Tower/Commercial Bay, ASB North Wharf, Downtown Car Park) and Wellington CBD (Bowen Campus, Defence House, Terrace towers) — approximately 70-75% Auckland / 25-30% Wellington by portfolio value, with Wellington's relative weight declining as Auckland development and capital-partnering activity accelerates

competitive_position.market_position: Largest listed owner/developer of premium CBD office real estate in New Zealand; effectively the only NZX-listed REIT with a pure-play, scaled premium-grade Auckland/Wellington CBD office concentration — peers are diversified away from office (KPG mixes retail/office including Sylvia Park mall; GMT is almost entirely industrial/logistics; ARG is 52% industrial/38% office/10% large-format retail; IPL is large-format retail; SPG is diversified office/industrial). This makes Precinct the primary vehicle for investors wanting direct exposure to the Auckland/Wellington office cycle, for better or worse.

moat_factors.factor: Scarcity of premium/Green Star CBD stock
moat_factors.description: Precinct owns a disproportionate share of Auckland's small pool of premium-grade, highly sustainable CBD towers (PwC Tower, Commercial Bay, HSBC Tower); flight-to-quality leasing trends (10.3% contract rent growth in 1H26, >25,000 sqm leased) are concentrating tenant demand into exactly this stock, and new premium supply is scarce and slow to build (multi-year consenting/construction lead times)

Ownership of entire mixed-use precincts (Commercial Bay, Bowen Campus, Wynyard Quarter) lets Precinct curate retail/hospitality/workspace amenity that smaller single-building owners cannot match, reinforcing tenant demand and rental premiums

Track record of $2.6bn+ developed since 2017 and active use of the Fast Track consenting pathway (Downtown Car Park) gives Precinct a structural edge in bringing new premium supply to market ahead of competitors, though this is capital- and execution-intensive

Repeat transactions with GIC (PPILP, ASB North Wharf) and a newly signed PAG partnership (PwC Tower) evidence a growing reputation as a credible local operating partner for global capital, expanding the effective balance sheet available for growth without proportional dilution

6.1-year WALT and government/blue-chip corporate tenant base underpin income durability, though large single tenants (e.g. MFAT at Molesworth Street, government agencies at Bowen Campus) create concentration risk

weaknesses: Office-only concentration removes the diversification benefit peers get from industrial/large-format-retail exposure, which have generally out-performed office through the recent cap-rate cycle
Wellington sub-portfolio carries structural government-tenant concentration exposed to public-sector downsizing, a risk KPG, GMT and ARG do not share to the same degree

High reliance on episodic, large-ticket capital-partner transactions (GIC, PAG) to fund growth and reduce gearing — a less repeatable, less diversified funding model than continuous retail-driven asset trusts

Complex stapled-entity/PIE structure and NCI accounting (PPIL non-controlling interest, currently a large negative equity balance) add reporting complexity for investors relative to simple single-trust REIT peers

growth_drivers: Auckland premium office leasing momentum — 10.3% contract rent growth and >25,000 sqm leased in 1H FY26, well above recent years, with further mark-to-market reversion available across the book

Downtown Car Park redevelopment — Fast Track resource consent lodged, ECI contractor arrangement targeted Q1 CY2026, ~50% of office NLA in pre-commitment negotiations, Stage 1 commitment targeted Q4 CY2026; positioned to set a new premium-office benchmark and reinforce the Commercial Bay precinct

Capital-partnering flywheel — PwC Tower 50:50 JV with PAG at a $600m headline valuation (announced June 2026, settling H1 FY27 subject to OIO) and the GIC-backed PPILP partnership (now ~$0.9bn including ASB North Wharf, ~80% Auckland-weighted) recycle capital into fee income and free the balance sheet for further development, with management targeting ~$4-5bn of capital partnerships over the medium term and ~20% of capital allocated to investment partnerships

Living-sector diversification — purpose-built student accommodation pipeline now 1,602 beds across two sites (22 Stanley Street with Keppel, and newly committed 256 Queen Street), plus residential build-to-sell projects (Pillars, Dominion/Valley Roads, York House, Westhaven with Orams) — a new, less cyclical NZ asset class for Precinct
Molesworth Street completion (practical completion Jan 2026, MFAT as anchor tenant) and improved Precinct Flex profitability post the FY25 business reset

NZ interest-rate easing/OCR cycle — lower funding costs support FFO growth directly (weighted average interest rate before swaps fell from 5.20% at Jun-25 to 4.41% at Dec-25) and could support cap-rate stabilisation or compression over time
Government's Investment Boost tax incentive cited by management as a tailwind to near-term earnings outlook

business.description: Despite Precinct's premium-grade advantage (flight-to-quality is currently a tailwind), a structural shift to lower office utilisation across the wider economy remains a multi-year overhang on aggregate CBD office demand and could eventually cap rental growth even for prime stock

The core public service is targeted to shrink from ~63,700 to ~55,000 FTEs by July 2029 (~14% reduction), with ~172,000 sqm / 13,500 employees of government leases expiring 2026-2028 across central Wellington; Precinct's Wellington book (Bowen Campus, Defence House, AON Centre-Wgtn, Terrace towers, ~25-30% of the portfolio) is directly exposed to non-renewal, downsizing or relocation decisions by government tenants, and CEO Scott Pritchard has explicitly flagged Wellington as 'more challenging' even as Auckland outperforms
Individual towers (PwC Tower, Molesworth Street/MFAT, Bowen Campus tenants) represent large blocks of income; loss or downsizing of a single anchor tenant has an outsized earnings impact

Downtown Car Park is a very large, multi-year, capital-hungry redevelopment still in preliminary design/consenting with only ~50% of office NLA in pre-commitment talks; the 1,602-bed student accommodation pipeline and residential build-to-sell projects add further construction, leasing and cost-overrun risk concurrently

The growth/de-gearing strategy depends on continuing to find willing global institutional partners (GIC, PAG) at attractive pricing; a cooling in offshore institutional appetite for NZ commercial real estate would stall the capital-recycling flywheel and force Precinct back toward balance-sheet funding or slower growth

financial.description: Pro forma gearing 33.7% at 31-Dec-2025 after using hotel/22 Stanley Street sale proceeds to repay debt; $1,495m of drawn debt with weighted average term to maturity of only 2.8 years means Precinct must continuously refinance in a still-elevated global rate environment; August 2025 refinance of $268m into a $275m Aug-2030 facility shows access to markets, but concentration in near-dated maturities (2026-2028) remains

Weighted average interest rate before swaps fell to 4.41% at Dec-2025 from 5.20% at Jun-2025 on lower base rates and refinancing, a tailwind to FFO, but bank debt is priced off floating BKBM plus margin, so any resumption of rate hikes (RBNZ lifted OCR 25bp to 2.50% in July 2026, with further hikes flagged into September/October 2026) would pressure interest costs and could also stall the cap-rate recovery

The $325m equity raise (October-November 2025, upsized SPP) lifted weighted average shares from 1,586.9m (1H25) to 1,692.6m (1H26), directly contributing to FFO per security falling from 3.47 cps to 3.18 cps year-on-year even as absolute FFO dollars were only modestly lower; further large raises to fund Downtown Car Park or student accommodation would extend this dilution

PPIL (management entity) carries persistent negative equity as presented non-controlling interest (-$61.4m at Dec-2025) under the stapled-entity consolidation convention; while economically PPNZ and PPIL trade only as one security, the accounting and PIE/withholding tax mechanics (imputation credits, supplementary dividends for non-residents) add complexity that can obscure underlying per-security economics for less experienced investors

regulatory.risk: OIO approval risk on PwC Tower JV
regulatory.description: The PAG 50:50 JV to acquire/sell down PwC Tower (headline $600m) is conditional on Overseas Investment Office approval and is not due to settle until H1 FY27 — deal risk exists until cleared

Downtown Car Park relies on the government's Fast Track Approvals regime for timely resource consent; any change to that regime or delays in the roughly six-month expected consent process would push out the development timetable

macro.description: Weighted average capitalisation rate across the wholly-owned investment portfolio was ~5.8% at 30 June 2025; every ~25bp of further cap-rate expansion mechanically reduces portfolio valuation and NTA by a low-to-mid single-digit percentage given the size of the property book (~$2.8bn wholly-owned investment properties plus ~$0.45bn development properties). NTA has already fallen from $1.21 (FY25) to $1.18/security (1H26) despite an internal review indicating 'no material movement' in the half; a resumption of the FY2023-25 devaluation cycle (statutory losses driven by cap-rate expansion) remains the single largest swing factor for reported equity

macro.risk: NZ commercial property cycle / economic recovery pace
macro.description: Management characterises the NZ economy as only now 'beginning to transition into the early stages of a recovery'; a slower-than-expected recovery in business investment and occupier demand would delay the absorption rebound CBRE and others expect through 2026-2028

OCR troughed and has begun rising again (2.50% as at July 2026, first hike since May 2023, with further hikes flagged), a reversal from the easing cycle that had been supporting valuations and funding costs through FY2025/26

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ commercial property outlook is improving but uneven: premium-grade Auckland CBD office is outperforming (constrained new supply, strong flight-to-quality leasing demand, 10.3% contract rent growth), while Wellington remains structurally challenged by public-sector downsizing. Broader occupier demand is expected to lift materially later in 2026 with a stronger absorption rebound into 2028, per CBRE's 2026 outlook, though a 'wait-and-see' sentiment has delayed the upswing.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High — office valuations and rents are sensitive to the economic and interest-rate cycle; Precinct's FY2023-25 experienced material devaluations as cap rates expanded, and the stock's reported earnings and NTA can swing sharply with property valuation movements even when underlying FFO is stable
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High — both directly (floating-rate bank debt priced off BKBM plus margin, ~2.8-year weighted average debt maturity requiring continuous refinancing) and indirectly via commercial property capitalisation rates, which move inversely with long-term interest rate expectations
key_input_costs: Construction/build costs for the development pipeline (Downtown Car Park, student accommodation, residential build-to-sell)
Debt funding costs (bank margins, bond coupons, US private placement costs)

recent_developments.event: Precinct agreed to sell a 50% interest in PwC Tower to Hong Kong-based global investor PAG, establishing a new investment partnership at a $600m headline valuation for the tower — the largest single-asset deal in Auckland CBD office market history; Precinct retains 50% and continues as investment/asset manager for a fee; settlement expected H1 FY27, conditional on OIO approval

PPILP (Precinct's GIC-anchored investment partnership) settled the $205m acquisition of ASB North Wharf in Wynyard Quarter from Kiwi Property Group after clearing OIO conditions in early 2026; lifts the partnership to ~$0.9bn in value, ~80% Auckland-weighted, with Precinct retaining a 24.9% interest

H1 FY2026 result released (six months to 31-Dec-2025): FFO 3.18 cps (down from 3.47 cps 1H25, partly equity-raise dilution), NTA $1.18/security (down from $1.21 at FY25), total comprehensive income nil, occupancy 97%, WALT 6.1 years, 10.3% contract rent growth, >25,000 sqm leased. FY26 guidance reaffirmed: 6.75 cps dividend, 7.30-7.50 cps FFO

Amora Hotel Wellington sale back settled ($15m); post-balance-date, InterContinental Auckland hotel and 22 Stanley Street also settled, with proceeds used to repay bank debt, taking pro forma gearing to 33.7% at 31-Dec-2025 (Precinct retains 20% of 22 Stanley Street alongside Keppel and continues as development manager for the 964-bed student accommodation project)

$325m equity raise completed ($285m institutional placement plus an oversubscribed retail SPP upsized to $40m), funding the growth pipeline including the newly committed 256 Queen Street student accommodation project; the raise triggered conversion-price-cap resets on the PCTHB/PCTHC convertible notes
Molesworth Street office development (Wellington) achieved practical completion, with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade becoming Precinct's largest single tenant
Refinanced $268m of bank loans maturing in 2026 with $275m of new facilities maturing 2030, plus secured a further $75m of bank liquidity

FY2026 full-year result (year ended 30-Jun-2026) due for release, with a live webcast — not yet published as of this analysis (24-Aug-2026); this will be the first full read on FY26 FFO/dividend delivery against 7.30-7.50 cps guidance and confirm year-end gearing, NTA and portfolio valuation movements

items.notes: Unchanged from FY2025 actual (6.75 cps) and from guidance provided at the FY25 result

Implies an FFO payout ratio of 90-92% against the 6.75 cps dividend; would represent growth versus FY2025 actual FFO of 7.10 cps if achieved, despite the FY26 equity raise dilution already reflected in the 1H26 run-rate (3.18 cps)

items.target: Qualitative — supportive to FY26 FFO delivery
items.notes: Management cited lower funding costs from recent capital management (refinancing, debt paydown from hotel/22 Stanley St proceeds), increasing income from Molesworth Street completion and the ASB North Wharf acquisition, revenue recognition from student accommodation projects, and NZ government's Investment Boost tax measure as the specific tailwinds underpinning H2 FFO

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Scott Pritchard: the investment portfolio 'continued to perform well, delivering underlying income growth,' with Auckland office like-for-like FFO growth of 3.0% (adjusted for occupancy/one-offs) versus a 'more challenging' Wellington market; Commercial Bay retail FFO up 2.5% with moving annual turnover up 6.2%. Leasing progress ('exceptional') and the $325m equity raise (oversubscribed) were highlighted as positioning the business for 'sustained earnings growth' via continued capital partnering. Management explicitly frames the NZ economy as only in the 'early stages of a recovery.'

bull_case: Genuine flight-to-quality tailwind in Auckland — 10.3% contract rent growth and record leasing volumes (>25,000 sqm in a single half) show Precinct's premium-grade scarcity advantage is currently working in its favour, not against it, with further mark-to-market rent reversion still available

Capital-partnering flywheel is now proven and scaling — the PAG deal on PwC Tower ($600m headline) and the GIC-anchored PPILP partnership (~$0.9bn, ASB North Wharf just added) demonstrate real institutional demand for Precinct-managed NZ CBD assets, recycling capital into fee income and de-risking the balance sheet (pro forma gearing down to 33.7%) while funding the development pipeline without pure dilution

Multi-year development pipeline (Downtown Car Park, 1,602 student accommodation beds, Molesworth Street just delivered) offers embedded medium-term earnings growth that is largely pre-let or de-risked through capital partnering before major capital is committed

Falling funding costs (weighted average interest rate before swaps down from 5.20% to 4.41% in six months) directly support FFO even before any cap-rate recovery, and NZ rate normalisation/economic recovery (per CBRE, occupier demand absorption expected to strengthen through 2026-2028) is a call-option on further NTA stabilisation or growth

Reaffirmed FY26 guidance (6.75 cps dividend, 7.30-7.50 cps FFO) despite a large equity raise mid-year signals management confidence in near-term earnings visibility ahead of the 27-Aug-2026 FY26 result
bear_case: Wellington government-tenant exposure is a live, quantifiable headwind — core public service FTEs are targeted to fall ~14% by July 2029 with ~172,000 sqm of Wellington government leases expiring 2026-2028, directly threatening income and occupancy at Bowen Campus, Defence House and other Wellington assets that management itself calls 'more challenging'

NTA has already fallen from $1.21 to $1.18/security in just six months and remains highly sensitive to a resumption of cap-rate expansion; the FY2023-25 devaluation cycle shows how quickly statutory equity can be eroded, and an OCR that is now rising again (2.50% July 2026, more hikes flagged) works against the cap-rate compression bulls are hoping for

FFO per security fell year-on-year (3.47 cps to 3.18 cps) — the $325m equity raise diluted per-security metrics even as headline FFO dollars held up, and further large capital raises to fund Downtown Car Park or student accommodation could repeat this pattern

Downtown Car Park and the student accommodation pipeline are large, multi-year, execution-heavy commitments (only ~50% of Downtown office NLA pre-committed as of Feb-2026, construction start still subject to preconditions) with meaningful cost-overrun, leasing and timing risk before they contribute earnings

The growth model is structurally dependent on continued appetite from a small number of large global institutional partners (GIC, PAG); a pullback in offshore capital demand for NZ real estate — plausible given NZ's small, illiquid market and OIO approval frictions — would stall the capital-recycling flywheel central to the current strategy
